sentences.text: Eothoracosaurus is an extinct genus of eusuchian crocodylomorphs found in the Eastern United States during the Late Cretaceous.

The name combines "Thoracosaurus" with the prefix "eos" meaning dawn, reflecting its earlier appearance in the fossil record compared to its relative, while the species name mississippiensis refers to the state of Mississippi where the holotype was found.
This animal possessed a strongly elongated skull similar to the modern gharial, which grew notably broader towards the back of the head.
The holotype, defined as the specimen the species is based on, consisted of a skull and postcrania discovered in 1931 and formally described by Kenneth Carpenter in 1983.
Christopher Brochu reexamined the material in 2004 and established the separate genus Eothoracosaurus due to substantial differences from other thoracosaurs.
Eothoracosaurus is associated with marine environments and coastal habitats, likely living in and around shallow marine areas.
It likely fed on fish and cephalopods.

The preserved teeth were slender, conical, and fairly evenly spaced, with the premaxilla containing five teeth where the first four were roughly equal in size and the fifth was notably smaller, while the maxillae contained 21 to 22 teeth on each side.
The animal lived during the Campanian to Maastrichtian stages, from 83.6 to 66 million years ago.
Research by Boerman et al. (2026) interprets the endocranial anatomy as consistent with a marine ecology and a lack of capability for deep diving.

Eothoracosaurus is classified within the family Gavialidae, though recent studies combining morphological, molecular, and stratigraphic data suggest that thoracosaurs like Eothoracosaurus were basal, non-crocodylian eusuchians rather than gavialoids.
